tldr: We proposed a framework that uses a local LLM and sequential graph purging to fully automate the construction of a semantic robot knowledge base aligned with any arbitrary task ontology, directly from URDF files that contain only geometric and kinematic data.
hero_caption: Overall processing flow of URDF2Ontology. The outer loop processes sensors, end-effectors, locomotion mechanisms, and body segments in order. Each pass performs extraction (blue), semantic typing (yellow), and abstraction/ontology assertion (green), followed by purging the processed nodes from the graph to prevent context window saturation.
overview:
In multi-robot fleets where heterogeneous robots collaborate, fleet management systems must symbolically understand each robot's physical capabilities—such as what sensors, arms, or locomotion systems it possesses—to allocate tasks effectively. However, the standard Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) contains only low-level numerical joint-link kinematic connections, lacking high-level semantics such as "this is a gripper" or "this is a camera." Historically, mapping URDF to ontologies like KnowRob required extensive manual authoring, posing a significant bottleneck.

To address this challenge, the authors propose URDF2Ontology, an automated neurosymbolic framework that transforms raw URDF files into robot embodiment ontologies (OWL ABoxes). Passing an entire URDF into an LLM at once leads to token explosion and hallucinations. Therefore, the framework adopts an ordered multi-pass pipeline based on robot morphological features—extracting peripheral sensors, end-effectors, locomotion assemblies, and serial body segments step-by-step—and iteratively purges processed sub-graphs from the kinematic tree. Furthermore, it employs a morphology-aware dual-track architecture: a bottom-up Tree Track for branching structures and a top-down Chain Track for serial limbs, hierarchically grounding components into any user-provided taxonomy (TBox).

Evaluated on five diverse platforms—the Solo quadruped, RB-VOGUI+ wheeled mobile manipulator, PR2, iCub full-scale humanoid, and Ingenuity Mars helicopter—using a local 20B open-weight LLM, the framework achieved highly accurate structural extraction and conceptual classification, demonstrating a substantial reduction in manual domain engineering overhead.
contributions: Established a multi-pass pipeline that generates ontologies while preventing LLM context window saturation by sequentially purging processed nodes from the URDF kinematic graph.
Proposed a morphology-aware dual-track architecture combining bottom-up aggregation for branching assemblies (sensors, grippers) with top-down decomposition for serial limbs (arms, head).
Achieved a taxonomy-agnostic design capable of aligning with arbitrary, user-specified ontology schemas (TBoxes) via iterative hierarchical constrained prompting without schema lock-in.
Demonstrated practical extraction accuracy across heterogeneous robot embodiments using only a local open-weight 20B parameter LLM, without cloud APIs or fine-tuning.

sections.heading: How do we bridge the robot's physical body with symbolic reasoning?
sections.summary: Task allocation across heterogeneous robot fleets requires grounding physical capabilities into symbols, yet URDF files provide purely low-level kinematics lacking semantics. To eliminate manual ontology engineering, we propose URDF2Ontology, which automatically generates arbitrary grounded ontologies from URDFs using a local LLM.
sections.details:
When robots collaborate in complex, real-world tasks, fleet management systems must know which platform possesses a camera and which platform has grasping capabilities. However, the standard Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) is tailored for dynamic simulation and kinematic calculation, detailing only parent-child relationships between rigid links and joints along with mesh file paths. Link names rely on designer-specific conventions and cryptic abbreviations (e.g., HL_KFE), making it extremely difficult for static rule-based parsers to infer that a given component is a rear-left knee joint.

While modern Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong commonsense reasoning, feeding an entire large, complex URDF text directly overwhelms the context window, scattering attention and triggering severe structural misinterpretations and hallucinations. Moreover, unlike conventional methods bound to a single rigid ontology, there was no flexible mechanism to adapt to the diverse classification schemas used by researchers (such as KnowRob, SOMA, or custom ontologies).

To solve this, the proposed approach combines sequential graph purging—processing from peripheral leaves inward while peeling away graph nodes—with a dual-track architecture tailored for branching and serial structures. This enables even a lightweight local LLM to accurately interpret URDF kinematics and build verifiable knowledge bases grounded in Description Logic.

sections.heading: At the intersection of knowledge representation and LLM grounding
sections.summary: While knowledge representation research has long developed robot ontologies, manual mapping has remained a bottleneck. Conversely, LLM applications in robotics have focused largely on 3D scene grounding, leaving the formal symbolic grounding of robot embodiment underexplored.
sections.details:
Related work broadly divides into two main streams.

### Robot Embodiment Models in Knowledge Representation
In robotics knowledge representation, standard ontologies such as IEEE 1872 (CORA, RTR), KnowRob, and SOMA exist. While they formally define tasks, environments, and robot capabilities, bridging the semantic gap between low-level URDF files and these high-level ontologies has historically relied on labor-intensive manual authoring by knowledge engineers. Approaches like SRDL (Semantic Robot Description Language) produced 1-to-1 mappings of URDF elements, but merely turning a continuous joint into an instance of a `RevoluteJoint` class fails to provide functional classification, such as identifying that a joint actuates a gripper finger.

### Semantic Grounding via LLMs in Robotics
Recent research heavily applies LLMs to construct semantic maps from 3D scene descriptions and point clouds. In embodiment modeling, frameworks like EMOS have used LLMs to generate unstructured natural language "resumes" from URDFs for task assignment. However, natural language summaries lose explicit topological sub-part hierarchies (e.g., an arm containing a forearm terminating in a gripper), preventing the formal verification of physical constraints and integration with Description Logic reasoners. This work bridges that gap through a neurosymbolic approach combining LLM flexibility with formal ontological rigor.

sections.heading: The big picture: Graph purging and neurosymbolic guardrails
sections.summary: We strip physical parameters from the raw URDF into a pure kinematic graph and process it in four sequential passes: sensors, end-effectors, locomotion, and body segments. Each step stabilizes LLM reasoning with guardrails like majority voting and hierarchical classification constraints.
sections.details:
### Problem Formulation and Outer Loop
Raw URDF files contain extensive information unnecessary for semantic classification, such as mesh filenames and inertia tensors, which waste LLM context tokens. The framework first strips these away to extract a directed acyclic graph $G_{\mathrm{URDF}} = (V_L, E_J)$, where $V_L$ represents link nodes and $E_J$ represents joint edges. The objective is to automatically instantiate an Assertional Box (ABox) of individuals $I$, concept assertions, and role assertions, governed by an expert-provided Terminological Box (TBox: concept set $C$ and relation set $R$).

URDF2Ontology processes the graph across four ordered passes reflecting canonical robot anatomy:
- **Pass 1 (Sensors)**: Typically located at the leaf nodes of the kinematic tree, these are extracted first to eliminate peripheral clutter.
- **Pass 2 (End-Effectors)**: Targets grippers and tool assemblies that become leaf structures after sensor removal.
- **Pass 3 (Locomotion)**: Extracts wheel assemblies, track bases, or leg mounts governing mobility.
- **Pass 4+ (Body Segments)**: Resolves the remaining core kinematic chains, such as arms, heads, and torso, once peripheral components are cleared.

After each pass $k$, the extracted sub-graph $G'$ is asserted into the ontology and immediately purged from the base graph: $G^{(k)} = \mathrm{Purge}(G^{(k-1)}, G')$. Consequently, link count $|V_L|$ decreases across passes, drastically shrinking the LLM's search space and preventing context saturation.

### Three Neurosymbolic Guardrails
To ensure robustness in LLM outputs, three guardrails are enforced:
- **Majority Voting**: Samples $K$ responses at temperature $T > 0$, adopting outputs only when meeting a consensus threshold (e.g., $\tau \ge 0.6$).
- **Context-Aware Batching**: Restricts the prompt to the local sub-graph neighborhood surrounding target candidate nodes rather than presenting the entire graph.
- **Iterative Hierarchical Classification**: Instead of exposing the entire ontology concept space at once, the LLM drills down child concepts level-by-level along the TBox tree ($C^{(0)} \supset C^{(1)} \supset \dots \supset C^{(d)}$). This strictly eliminates out-of-vocabulary hallucinations.

captions.P3: Kinematic link graph extracted from the PR2 robot's right arm sub-tree. Numerous serial and parallel links extend from base_link to peripheral cameras and gripper fingertips, which are iteratively purged as they are asserted into the ontology.

sections.heading: Inside the pipeline: Dual tracks for branching trees and serial chains
sections.summary: Within each pass, the inner loop executes Extraction (Phase I), Semantic Typing (Phase II), and Abstraction & Graph Purging (Phase III). Phase II uniquely routes branching assemblies through the bottom-up Tree Track and serial limbs through the top-down Chain Track.
sections.details:
The inner loop of each pass consists of three distinct phases:

### Phase I: Extraction
The LLM inspects current leaf nodes to identify candidates matching the target pass category. It then traverses ancestor paths $P(v_{\mathrm{leaf}})$ back toward the root link, prompting the LLM to identify the anatomical mount link that interfaces with the base platform. Severing the tree at this mount isolates candidate sub-graphs $G_{\mathrm{cand}}$ without pulling in extraneous body links.

### Phase II.A: Tree Track (Bottom-Up Aggregation)
Applied to branching assemblies emerging from a common mount, such as multi-finger grippers, sensor clusters, or multi-wheel bases:
- **Step 1 (Branch Typing)**: Hierarchically classifies isolated branch sub-graphs (e.g., mapping a distal tip link to `Finger` and an optical origin to `ToolCenterPoint`).
- **Step 2 (Branch Clustering)**: Evaluates whether multiple branches connected to the same mount form a unified functional unit (e.g., a two-finger gripper).
- **Step 3 (Macro Assembly Typing)**: Classifies the clustered macro assembly into a high-level concept (e.g., `TwoFingerGripper`). Retaining both component branches and the macro structure preserves high-resolution domain knowledge.

### Phase II.B: Chain Track (Top-Down Decomposition)
Applied to serial, non-branching linkages in Pass 4+, such as arms, necks, and torsos:
- **Step 1 (Macro Chain Typing)**: First classifies the entire continuous serial chain as a high-level concept (e.g., `Arm`).
- **Step 2 (Chain Partitioning)**: Leverages joint kinematic types and naming heuristics to identify functional segment boundaries, decomposing the chain into contiguous sub-segments.
- **Step 3 (Segment Typing)**: Classifies each sub-segment into specific anatomical concepts (e.g., `UpperArm`, `Forearm`, `Wrist`). Having the global context established in Step 1 ensures accurate classification even when intermediate link names are cryptic.
- **Step 4 (Segment Clustering)**: Consolidates over-partitioned or parallel structures back into cohesive physical limb segments.

### Phase III: Abstraction & Graph Purging
Assigns unambiguous individual URIs using LLM generation (Step 1, e.g., `pr2_right_arm`), verifies graph integrity to prevent disconnected orphan links (Step 2), and populates the OWL ABox with concept and role assertions (`hasSubPart`, `isMountedOn`, etc., Step 3). Finally, the asserted sub-graph is purged from the working graph before passing execution to the next pass.

captions.P6: Ontology graph generated in Phase III for the PR2 gripper region. Under the macro individual TwoFingerGripper, two Finger instances and a ToolCenterPoint are connected via hasSubPart, while an Accelerometer extracted during Pass 1 is linked via hasSubsystem.

sections.heading: Experiments across real robot URDFs: From quadrupeds to dense humanoids
sections.summary: We evaluated the framework on Solo (quadruped), RB-VOGUI+ (mobile manipulator), PR2, iCub (humanoid), and Ingenuity (Mars helicopter) using a local 20B LLM. Excluding iCub's high-density tactile skin cells, it achieved highly accurate structural extraction and ontology population across all platforms.
sections.details:
Experiments were run locally on Ubuntu 24.04 (Intel Core i7-12850HX, NVIDIA RTX A4500 16GB GPU) using an open-weight model, `gpt-oss:20b` (via Ollama), evaluating mapping fidelity against a custom modular OWL robotics taxonomy.

### Platform-Specific Results
- **Solo (Quadruped)**: Consolidated 13 links into 5 individuals. Despite cryptic joint labels such as "HL_KFE", it accurately inferred limb segments and ground-contact tips, asserting four `ArticulatedLeg` instances under a `QuadrupedalBase`.
- **RB-VOGUI+ (Mobile Manipulator)**: Extracted 34 individuals from 53 links, cleanly separating the 4-wheel omnidirectional drive base from the manipulator arm. Although the arm contained a parallel kinematic branch in the URDF, Chain Track segment clustering correctly unified it into a single `SerialManipulatorArm` rather than splitting it into distinct arms.
- **PR2 (Mobile Manipulator)**: Accurately generated 61 individuals from 82 links. It partitioned the 7-DOF arm into shoulder, upper arm, forearm, and wrist segments, correctly extracted the `PanTiltHead`, and captured caster assemblies. Lexical fidelity was notable: a link named "laser" was mapped directly to `LaserRangeFinder`.
- **iCub (High-Density Humanoid)**: The ultimate stress test. An initial attempt including 150 individual tactile skin sensor cells caused LLM context overflow, causing the model to hallucinate and dump raw code. This failure reinforces the paper's core premise: massive URDFs cannot be passed to an LLM without decomposition. When skin cells were omitted (134 links), the framework synthesized 19 functional sensors from 30 link frames and clustered 5-finger hands into distinct `DexterousHand` assemblies, generating 84 validated individuals.
- **Ingenuity (Mars Helicopter)**: Extracted 9 individuals from 13 links. Coaxial counter-rotating blades were grouped into a `RotorAssembly`, and passive landing struts were recognized as leg support structures from joint topology.

sections.heading: Open challenges: Naming reliance and hybrid leg anatomy
sections.summary: Key limitations include degraded performance when link names are obfuscated or purely numerical, conceptual coarsening from static TBoxes, handling hybrid serial-branching structures in legged robots, and the absence of run-time Description Logic reasoner feedback.
sections.details:
While the framework proved effective, several limitations were identified:

- **Reliance on Lexical Identifiers**: Although kinematic graph topology and joint actuation types guide reasoning, the LLM still relies on semantic hints within link identifiers. When URDF files use fully obfuscated or arbitrary numerical labels (e.g., `link_01`), functional inference fails much as it would for a human engineer.
- **Static Schema and Vocabulary Granularity**: Highly specialized sensors or custom actuators not defined in the input TBox are coarse-grained into broader parent concepts. Furthermore, concept descriptions (`rdfs:comment`) were omitted from prompts to manage token limits, trading deep semantic nuance for efficiency.
- **Legged Locomotion Granularity**: In the current implementation, Pass 3 (Locomotion) relies solely on the Tree Track, purging quadruped legs as monolithic assemblies. However, animal-like legs also possess serial link chains (thigh, shank). A hybrid strategy integrating Chain Track decomposition into locomotion passes is needed.
- **Lack of Dynamic Reasoner Feedback**: The pipeline does not yet interface with run-time Description Logic reasoners (such as HermiT or Pellet) to validate asserted individuals against ontological axioms (e.g., disjointness constraints) in real time to trigger automated LLM self-correction loops.

sections.heading: Conclusion and what lies ahead
sections.summary: URDF2Ontology establishes a fully automated pipeline to turn raw URDF files into verifiable OWL ontologies using sequential graph purging and morphology-aware dual tracks. Future work aims to integrate dynamic reasoner validation and extract Gazebo simulation parameters.
sections.details:
This work introduced URDF2Ontology, an automated neurosymbolic framework that transforms raw URDF kinematics into grounded OWL ontologies aligned with arbitrary user-defined TBox schemas.

By sequentially purging sub-graphs from distal leaves inward, the pipeline prevents context window saturation, enabling even local LLMs to parse intricate kinematic structures like humanoids. Furthermore, the dual-track architecture cleanly separates branching assemblies from serial chains, successfully preserving both low-level constituent parts and high-level macro assemblies within the knowledge base.

Future avenues include real-time logical validation with OWL reasoners to prompt LLMs for self-repair upon axiom conflicts, parsing Gazebo simulation plugins to extract fine-grained capabilities like sensor field-of-view and gripper payload limits, and closing the loop by automatically generating Semantic Robot Description Format (SRDF) configurations directly from populated ontologies.

takeaways: When parsing massive kinematic tree structures with LLMs, sequential graph purging—processing leaves first and removing completed nodes—is critical to preventing context window saturation.
Differentiating between branching assemblies (Tree Track: bottom-up aggregation) and continuous serial chains (Chain Track: top-down decomposition) perfectly captures diverse robot morphologies.
Hierarchical classification constraints that traverse user-defined TBox trees level-by-level strictly prevent out-of-vocabulary hallucinations.
Knowledge engineering can be reliably automated with local, open-weight 20B LLMs without cloud APIs or fine-tuning, provided prompt architecture and symbolic guardrails are tightly integrated.
limitations: Relies on meaningful lexical strings within URDF link and joint names, failing when kinematics are obfuscated with arbitrary numbers or non-descriptive labels (e.g., link_1, joint_a).
Lacks anatomical granularity for hybrid structures like legged robots, which branch from a base but internally feature serial chains (e.g., femur, tibia), coarsening them into monolithic assemblies.
Lacks real-time integration with OWL Description Logic reasoners, preventing automated run-time self-repair loops if asserted individuals violate schema axioms.
